summary: This experimental document describes how to use the OSPF-MANET interface in single-hop broadcast networks. It includes a way to detect such a network dynamically and covers operational considerations. It updates RFC 5820.

eli5.summary: A routing method made for roaming wireless groups is used where everyone can hear everyone. This explains how to notice that situation and behave well.

questions: ospf manet interface on broadcast network
how does smart peering use router priority
subtitle: How to run the OSPF-MANET interface on a network where every node reaches every other directly, and how to detect that situation.

tldr.problem: The OSPF broadcast model cannot describe single-hop networks, such as an Ethernet-like segment, where different pairs of nodes have different link metrics.
tldr.mechanism: The MANET interface is used as is, with the overlapping relay process switched off, smart peering guided by Router Priority, and a SingleHop flag plus a ModeChange timer that detect and manage the switch between single-hop and multi-hop modes.
tldr.outcome: No new on-the-wire changes are needed. The RFC is Experimental and updates RFC 5820.

today: RFC 7137 is an Experimental document that updates RFC 5820, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Use the MANET Interface Here
sections.content:
The OSPF-MANET interface (RFC 5820) treats every router-to-router connection as a point-to-point link, allows a link metric per neighbor, and uses the layer-2 broadcast and multicast of the media. The authors argue these traits help in other networks too, specifically single-hop broadcast networks where all nodes are directly connected but the cost between pairs of nodes may differ. An Ethernet interface is given as a good example of the connectivity model.

The OSPF broadcast model (RFC 2328) cannot describe those differing metrics accurately, so a point-to-multipoint description fits better. This document updates RFC 5820 with a simplified operation, which does not need overlapping relays, and a new heuristic for smart peering using Router Priority.
sections.eli5: If everyone in a room can talk to everyone but some friends are farther away, a list of individual distances describes things better than one big group label.

sections.title: Operation in Single-Hop Mode
sections.content:
The operation of the MANET interface does not change on a single-hop interface, but some enhancements can be simplified. The Overlapping Relay Discovery Process SHOULD NOT be run, and the A-bit SHOULD NOT be set by any node, so the set of Active Overlapping Relays is empty. The document uses already defined mechanisms and needs no additional on-the-wire changes.

An unsynchronized adjacency is one whose database synchronization is postponed but which is announced as FULL because reachability through the shortest path tree can be proven. In a single-hop network the check is simple: the adjacency to a peer MUST be advertised as FULL by at least one smart peer. Flooding SHOULD be enabled for all unsynchronized adjacencies so that all nodes can use all the LSAs received.
sections.eli5: Because everyone is already close, the extra helper steps are skipped. Friends only need to be told someone can reach each person, and then the news reaches all.

sections.title: Smart Peering with Router Priority
sections.content:
Smart peering reduces the need for a full mesh of adjacencies: a new adjacency is not required if the node is already reachable through the existing shortest path tree. This document gives a heuristic to use in step 3 of the smart peering state machine, in place of the original one in RFC 5820.

For the MANET interface, Router Priority is an 8-bit unsigned integer that decides which routers to form a FULL adjacency with. The router with the highest Router Priority takes precedence, and a tie goes to the highest Router ID. The heuristic checks that the number of adjacencies is below the configured maximum and that the neighbor has the highest (Router Priority, Router ID) combination. Routers SHOULD wait for the ModeChange timer to expire before running it, to avoid churn. The selected nodes are called smart peers, and a maximum of 2 adjacencies is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone holding hands with everyone, each person holds hands with only the top-ranked couple of friends, and ties are settled by who has the higher ID number.

sections.title: Detecting Single-Hop Networks and Changing Mode
sections.content:
Each node compares its 1-hop neighbors with its 2-hop neighborhood. If, for every 1-hop neighbor, the 2-hop set contains all the remaining 1-hop neighbors, the interface is single-hop. This is the Single-Hop Condition. A new SingleHop flag in the interface data structure is set when it holds and MUST be cleared when it stops holding.

A new ModeChange timer MUST be set whenever the flag changes. It is the time an interface SHOULD wait before switching modes, and it is RECOMMENDED to be set to Wait Time from RFC 2328.

Going to single-hop mode, once the timer expires the Router Priority heuristic MAY be run, and an adjacency MUST NOT go from FULL to 2-Way unless the simplified reachability check can be verified. Going back to multi-hop mode, the A-bit MUST be set if the condition fails because the 1-hop set grew without the 2-hop set growing, or because the 2-hop neighborhood shrank while keeping all earlier 1-hop neighbors. After the timer, the multi-hop operation of RFC 5820 takes over. When a node joins, the Designated Router and Backup Designated Router fields in the Hello packet MAY be used to tell it who the current smart peers are.
sections.eli5: Each kid checks if all their friends can also see each other. If so, they use the simple rules. If someone moves out of sight, they wait a bit and switch back to the careful rules.
